greek.name: Greek

signature.name: Glory
rules: Your heroes gain 25% more experience from battles they win (rounded down).

greek.summary: Disciplined hoplites, sky-borne griffins and the one-eyed giants of Thunder Quarry. The faction of The Three Beacons campaign; playable in skirmish too.

provenance.note: Roster provisionally reduced to one family per tier (Griffin at tier 3).

norse.name: Norse

signature.name: Berserk Fury
signature.summary: The fewer who stand, the harder they strike.
rules: In battle, a stack of yours with at most half of its starting creatures alive gains +2 Attack.

norse.summary: Barrow-risen Draugar, frost wolves, valkyries and the root-gnawing wyrms of the deep north. Playable in skirmish with proposed, unplaytested values.

provenance.note: Owner decision: Claude proposes every Norse number; labelled proposed.

egyptian.name: Egyptian
egyptian.summary: Sun-scarabs, jackal wardens, tireless ushabti and sphinxes of the river kingdoms. Playable in skirmish with proposed, unplaytested values.

signature.name: Afterlife
signature.summary: The fallen are called back from the west bank.
rules: After a battle you win, each of your stacks regains 20% of the creatures it lost in that battle (rounded down).
Never more than the stack lost; grants no experience, rewards or kills.

provenance.note: Owner request: every pantheon playable; Claude proposes every number; labelled proposed.

japanese.name: Japanese
japanese.summary: Fox spirits, river kappa, mountain tengu and the eight-headed Orochi of shrine and castle country. Playable in skirmish with proposed, unplaytested values.

signature.name: Harmony
rules: Counted when a battle starts: with 3 or more different creature families in your army, every stack gains +1 Defense.

provenance.note: Owner request: every pantheon playable; Claude proposes every number; labelled proposed.

celtic.name: Celtic
celtic.summary: Shape-shifting pooka, otherworld hounds, loch kelpies and the sea-giants of the hillforts. Playable in skirmish with proposed, unplaytested values.

signature.name: Shapeshifting
signature.summary: The old folk wear more than one skin.
rules: Creatures with Shapeshift (Pooka, Kelpie, Selkie, Horned Stag Spirit) change aspect at the start of their activation without spending it, once per activation.
Without this rite, Shapeshift spends the activation.

provenance.note: Owner request: every pantheon playable; Claude proposes every number; labelled proposed.

mesoamerican.name: Mesoamerican
mesoamerican.summary: Feathered serpents, jaguar spirits, eagle warriors and fire serpents of the temple cities. Playable in skirmish with proposed, unplaytested values.

signature.name: Offering
signature.summary: The sun is fed so that it rises.
rules: Once per week in each town with a Temple, offer creatures from the garrison or the visiting hero.
Gain 1 Favor per 125 Gold of their recruitment price (rounded down), at most 10 Favor per offering.
A hero cannot offer its last creature.

provenance.note: Owner request: every pantheon playable; Claude proposes every number; labelled proposed.

charge_guard.name: Charge Guard
charge_guard.summary: Braced shields blunt a cavalry charge.
charge_guard.exactRule: Ignore the attacker's charge bonus against this stack.
charge_guard.restriction: Does not negate the underlying melee strike or Offense.

shooter.name: Shooter
shooter.exactRule: Enables the stationary Shoot action; one ammunition per shot.
shooter.restriction: Cannot shoot while adjacent to an enemy or at a target beyond its range; half damage in the far half of its range; half damage in melee unless No Melee Penalty.

flight.name: Flight
flight.summary: Flies over obstacles and other stacks.
flight.exactRule: May cross blocked or occupied cells within its Speed.
flight.restriction: Requires a legal whole-footprint landing; no travel beyond Speed.

retaliation_2.name: Double Retaliation
retaliation_2.summary: Answers two melee attacks each round.
retaliation_2.restriction: Reset only at round start; a destroyed stack cannot retaliate.

retaliation_unlimited.name: Unlimited Retaliation
retaliation_unlimited.restriction: Dead or disabled stacks still cannot retaliate; no retaliation chains.

charge.name: Charge
charge.summary: Hits harder after a long approach.
charge.exactRule: +5% damage per hex traversed on the shortest legal approach, capped at +25%.
charge.restriction: Melee activation only; no charge on retaliation; detours cannot farm distance; negated by Charge Guard.

family_ward.name: Ward
family_ward.summary: Places a protective ward on a friendly stack.
family_ward.exactRule: Spend the activation: a friendly stack gains +3 Defense through the current and next round.
family_ward.restriction: One charge shared by the whole Temple Adept family per army per battle; no hero mana.

unyielding.name: Unyielding
unyielding.exactRule: Effective morale is at least +1, before the +3 cap.
unyielding.restriction: Does not create an extra roll, grant immunity, or affect allies.

wall_breaker.name: Wall Breaker
wall_breaker.summary: Can target fortifications in a siege.
wall_breaker.exactRule: Attacking a town: spend the activation and one shot to remove 1 structure HP from an intact wall, gate, tower or keep. No troop attack that activation.
wall_breaker.restriction: Besieging side only; not while engaged by an adjacent enemy; no effect in open-field battles.

shapeshift_hare.name: Shapeshift (Hare)
shapeshift_hare.summary: Slips into a hare’s shape to outrun the line.
shapeshift_hare.exactRule: Spend the activation to take the Hare aspect (-1 Defense, +2 Speed) or return to the normal aspect. With the Shapeshifting rite the change is free at the start of the activation, once per activation.
shapeshift_hare.restriction: Only the stack itself; lasts until it changes back or the battle ends. Speed changes affect movement at once and turn order from the next round; never adventure travel.

shapeshift_waterhorse.name: Shapeshift (Water-horse)
shapeshift_waterhorse.summary: Becomes the drowning horse of the loch.
shapeshift_waterhorse.exactRule: Spend the activation to take the Water-horse aspect (+2 Attack, -2 Defense) or return to the normal aspect. With the Shapeshifting rite the change is free at the start of the activation, once per activation.
shapeshift_waterhorse.restriction: Only the stack itself; lasts until it changes back or the battle ends. Speed changes affect movement at once and turn order from the next round; never adventure travel.

shapeshift_sealskin.name: Shapeshift (Seal-skin)
shapeshift_sealskin.summary: Pulls on the seal-skin and sets like a rock.
shapeshift_sealskin.exactRule: Spend the activation to take the Seal-skin aspect (+3 Defense, -2 Speed) or return to the normal aspect. With the Shapeshifting rite the change is free at the start of the activation, once per activation.
shapeshift_sealskin.restriction: Only the stack itself; lasts until it changes back or the battle ends. Speed changes affect movement at once and turn order from the next round; never adventure travel.

shapeshift_rut.name: Shapeshift (Rut)
shapeshift_rut.summary: The antlers lower; the forest charges.
shapeshift_rut.exactRule: Spend the activation to take the Rut aspect (+3 Attack, -3 Defense) or return to the normal aspect. With the Shapeshifting rite the change is free at the start of the activation, once per activation.
shapeshift_rut.restriction: Only the stack itself; lasts until it changes back or the battle ends. Speed changes affect movement at once and turn order from the next round; never adventure travel.

no_melee_penalty.name: No Melee Penalty
no_melee_penalty.summary: Fights at full strength up close.
no_melee_penalty.exactRule: Do not apply the shooter's 0.5 melee penalty.
no_melee_penalty.restriction: Ordinary ranged distance and wall limits still apply.

lore.hoplite.sourceNote: Greek hoplites are associated with armored infantry, a spear and shield, and fighting in close formation. Equipment and practice varied by place and period. This note does not establish troop price, formation bonus or recruitment speed.
sourceRefs: L01 — museum scholarship on Greek hoplite equipment
lore.hoplite.gameLore: The road to Asterion is lined with shields bearing names rather than royal crests. Each belongs to a household that promised someone would stand when the warning bells rang. Hoplites learn to hold a narrow path together, trusting the shield beside them as much as their own spear.
lore.hoplite.upgradeLore: Veteran Hoplites teach the pause before a charge reaches the line. Their distinction is practiced steadiness, not a divine transformation.

lore.peltast.sourceNote: Xenophon's Hellenica discusses Iphicrates and his peltasts in the Lechaeum campaign context. This supports an ancient light-troop tradition as inspiration; not every peltast fought identically or wore one uniform.
sourceRefs: L06 — Xenophon, Hellenica
lore.peltast.gameLore: Peltasts learn the hills before they learn the parade ground. They carry only what lets them cross a dry riverbed, find a gap between shields, and return before a heavier enemy can close. The best return with useful news and an unused last weapon.
lore.peltast.upgradeLore: Veteran Peltasts choose their own firing ground and carry additional ammunition — represented by the upgrade statistics, not an extra action.

lore.centaur.sourceNote: Ancient accounts include named centaurs such as Pholus and Chiron as well as hostile centaur encounters (Apollodorus, Library 2.5.4). Our grove-dwelling family is a fictional adaptation.
sourceRefs: L03 — Apollodorus, Library 2.5.4
lore.centaur.gameLore: The grove's covenant is written on neither parchment nor stone. Its terms are paths left open, springs left clean, and warnings answered before smoke reaches the canopy. Centaurs who ride with the polis follow an agreement between neighbors.
lore.centaur.upgradeLore: Sentinels know the old boundary routes and lead the first response when a covenant’s roads are threatened.

lore.griffin.sourceNote: Greek literary sources, including passages of Herodotus, tell of griffins associated with guarded gold. Griffin imagery is not exclusively Greek. The winged battlefield ally is a game interpretation.
sourceRefs: L05 — Herodotus
lore.griffin.gameLore: Above Griffin Pass, the nests face the first light. The first envoys brought gold and were driven from the cliffs; the next brought food and waited. The covenant began when a wounded fledgling was returned without chains.
lore.griffin.upgradeLore: Windcrest Griffins are experienced guardians of the highest nests. Their persistence is expressed by the retaliation rule, not invulnerability.

lore.cavalry.sourceNote: Xenophon's Cavalry Commander discusses horsemanship, terrain practice, supplies and command. It inspires trained mounted troops, not our exact charge modifier. 'Companion Cavalry' is a fictional upgrade name here.
sourceRefs: L07 — Xenophon, Cavalry Commander
lore.cavalry.gameLore: The court measures a rider by the condition of the horse at the journey’s end. Young cavalry learn patience before speed: which track will hold after rain, where a line can be approached, and when a charge would spend lives for nothing.
lore.cavalry.upgradeLore: Companion riders train together until the commander’s signal is almost unnecessary.

lore.temple_adept.sourceNote: This magical combat profession and its institution are original Pantheon Realms fiction. It is not a historical Greek military class, and no ancient source is claimed.
lore.temple_adept.gameLore: Temple Adepts keep the records that armies would rather forget: every promise made before a march and every name missing afterward. The light they carry into battle belongs to this world’s living gods.
lore.temple_adept.upgradeLore: Seers learn to place a brief ward over their companions. The rite is shared by the whole company — one family-wide charge.

lore.minotaur.sourceNote: Apollodorus describes the Minotaur in the story of Pasiphae and the Labyrinth. That named being is not a historical account of a recruitable species; our Minotaur people are a deliberate fantasy expansion.
sourceRefs: L02 — Apollodorus
lore.minotaur.gameLore: The wardens of the lower labyrinth remember a time when every corridor ended in a locked gate. They now carve their own signs into the stone, choosing who may enter and what may leave. Their loyalty is an agreement, not a property of their horns.
lore.minotaur.upgradeLore: A Labyrinth Warden is entrusted with the passages others must not lose. Its steadiness is the minimum-morale rule; it does not make the whole army fearless.

lore.cyclops.sourceNote: Hesiod's Theogony associates named Cyclopes with Zeus' thunder weapon, while Odyssey 9 presents Polyphemus in a different setting. Our siege specialist combines selected motifs as original fiction.
sourceRefs: L04 — Hesiod, Theogony; Homer, Odyssey 9
lore.cyclops.gameLore: Thunder Quarry is less a mine than a negotiation with the mountain. A Cyclops may spend a day shaping a single stone until it sits correctly in one vast hand. In battle, the same patience becomes a frightening economy of movement.
lore.cyclops.upgradeLore: Stormforged Cyclopes carry stones marked by the forge’s rites. The name adds no lightning damage.

lore.norse_draugr.sourceNote: The draugr is the restless dead of Old Norse saga literature, a corpse that keeps to its burial mound and is dangerous to the living. Accounts differ from saga to saga.
sourceRefs: Icelandic family sagas (e.g. Grettis saga) — to be verified
lore.norse_draugr.gameLore: The barrows above Frosthold were raised for warriors who died owing a debt. Some of them still stand guard over it. The living leave mead at the mound doors and do not ask what drinks it.
lore.norse_draugr.upgradeLore: The Deathless keep an oath older than the hold itself; nothing on a battlefield is frightening enough to break it.

lore.norse_frost_wolf.sourceNote: Wolves are prominent in Norse myth; the great wolf Fenrir, bound by the gods, is described in the Prose Edda. Our frost wolves are an original adaptation.
sourceRefs: Snorri Sturluson, Prose Edda (Gylfaginning) — to be verified
lore.norse_frost_wolf.gameLore: The wolves of the white valleys run beside the hold’s riders rather than under them. They are paid in the first share of every hunt, and they remember who pays.
lore.norse_frost_wolf.upgradeLore: Fenrir Wolves wear a broken link of chain as a collar. Nobody in the hold remembers who first put it there.

lore.norse_frost_troll.sourceNote: Trolls appear widely in Scandinavian folklore as large, dangerous beings of the mountains and wilds; the frost variety here is our invention.
sourceRefs: Scandinavian folklore collections — to be verified
lore.norse_frost_troll.gameLore: Frost trolls sleep through summer in caves that never thaw. The hold wakes them in autumn with drums and fresh meat, and sends them home before the thaw.
lore.norse_frost_troll.upgradeLore: The ancient trolls have ice grown into their skin like armor, and they are slower to anger and far slower to stop.

lore.norse_valkyrie.sourceNote: Valkyries — "choosers of the slain" — appear in Eddic and skaldic poetry as figures who decide who falls in battle and bring the chosen to Valhalla.
sourceRefs: Poetic Edda; Prose Edda — to be verified
lore.norse_valkyrie.gameLore: The hold’s valkyries are not goddesses; they are the women who survived the choosing and came back with wings. They fight where the line is about to break.
lore.norse_valkyrie.upgradeLore: Battle Valkyries have chosen before. They turn to meet a second attacker without looking.

lore.norse_lindworm.sourceNote: The lindworm is a serpentine dragon of Scandinavian and wider Germanic folklore; the Sigurd legend (Fáfnir) is carved on the Ramsund rock in Sweden.
sourceRefs: Ramsund carving; Völsunga saga — to be verified
lore.norse_lindworm.gameLore: Lindworms nest on the sea-cliffs where the spray freezes. A lindworm that has been fed from a hand will breathe frost for that hand, and for no one else.
lore.norse_lindworm.upgradeLore: Storm Lindworms are the ones that survived lightning; they bite as readily as they breathe.

lore.norse_jotunn.sourceNote: The jötnar are the giants of Norse myth, frequently in conflict with the gods yet also kin to them; they are named throughout the Eddas.
sourceRefs: Poetic Edda; Prose Edda — to be verified
lore.norse_jotunn.gameLore: A jotunn does not serve the hold. It keeps an agreement with it, renewed each winter by a gift the giants choose. This year it was a bell.
lore.norse_jotunn.upgradeLore: Runic Jotnar cut protections into their own stone bracers and will lend one to an ally who asks politely.

lore.norse_nidhogg_wyrm.sourceNote: Níðhöggr is the dragon that gnaws at the roots of the world-tree Yggdrasil in Eddic poetry; Jörmungandr is the world-serpent. Our wyrms borrow both names.
sourceRefs: Völuspá; Grímnismál — to be verified
lore.norse_nidhogg_wyrm.gameLore: Beneath the hold the roots of an old tree go down into warm dark water, and something down there gnaws. The priests call it a blessing that it has not yet finished.
lore.norse_nidhogg_wyrm.upgradeLore: World-Serpent Wyrms are sea-green and barnacled. Nothing moves them that they do not wish to be moved by.

lore.egyptian_sacred_scarab.sourceNote: The scarab (kheper) was a symbol of the rising sun and of renewal; the god Khepri was depicted as a scarab pushing the sun across the sky.
sourceRefs: Egyptian amulet traditions; Khepri iconography — to be verified
lore.egyptian_sacred_scarab.gameLore: Every morning the temple keepers count the scarabs that come up out of the sand. Every evening there are more of them than there were.
lore.egyptian_sacred_scarab.upgradeLore: Solar Scarabs have rolled the sun-disc once. The keepers say its warmth never quite leaves their shells.

lore.egyptian_jackal_guardian.sourceNote: Anubis, the jackal-headed god, was associated with embalming and the protection of the dead; jackals were linked with cemeteries on the desert edge.
sourceRefs: Egyptian funerary texts and tomb iconography — to be verified
lore.egyptian_jackal_guardian.gameLore: The Guardians were given jackal faces so the dead would know them at a glance. The living find the faces less reassuring.
lore.egyptian_jackal_guardian.upgradeLore: An Anubian Warden has guarded a king’s door for a lifetime. It no longer matters to him how close the thief gets.

lore.egyptian_ushabti.sourceNote: Ushabti (shabti) were small funerary figurines placed in tombs to perform work for the deceased in the afterlife.
sourceRefs: Book of the Dead, spell 6 — to be verified
lore.egyptian_ushabti.gameLore: Somebody has to answer when the call comes for labour in the next world. The ushabti answer in this one too, if the right words are painted on them.
lore.egyptian_ushabti.upgradeLore: Royal Ushabti were made by the hundred for a single king. They have never been told he is gone.

lore.egyptian_sphinx.sourceNote: Egyptian sphinxes — lions with the head of a king — were guardian figures at temples and tombs, the best known being the Great Sphinx of Giza.
sourceRefs: Giza plateau; temple avenue sphinxes — to be verified
lore.egyptian_sphinx.gameLore: The sphinxes on the terrace were stone once. Nobody in the city is old enough to say when that stopped being true.
lore.egyptian_sphinx.upgradeLore: The Great Sphinxes are the ones that grew wings. They still prefer to wait, but they no longer have to.

lore.egyptian_crocodile_beast.sourceNote: Sobek was a crocodile god linked with the Nile and its fertility; crocodiles were kept and mummified at his temples, for example at Kom Ombo.
sourceRefs: Kom Ombo temple; animal mummy finds — to be verified
lore.egyptian_crocodile_beast.gameLore: The river gives and the river takes. The pens are where the city keeps the part of the river that takes.
lore.egyptian_crocodile_beast.upgradeLore: A Sobek Warbeast wears its god’s sun-disc. The priests say that is why it never has to look where it is going.

lore.egyptian_bennu.sourceNote: The Bennu was a heron-like bird associated with the sun, creation and rebirth, venerated at Heliopolis; Greek writers later linked it with the phoenix.
sourceRefs: Heliopolitan tradition; Herodotus II.73 (phoenix) — to be verified
lore.egyptian_bennu.gameLore: The Bennu nests on the highest pillar in the city and leaves at dawn. The watchers on the walls have learned to follow where it flies.
lore.egyptian_bennu.upgradeLore: A Radiant Bennu has already died once in fire. It sees no reason to be afraid of anything smaller.

lore.egyptian_desert_colossus.sourceNote: Colossal royal statues such as the Colossi of Memnon and those of Ramesses II at Abu Simbel stood at temple entrances as images of the king.
sourceRefs: Colossi of Memnon; Abu Simbel — to be verified
lore.egyptian_desert_colossus.gameLore: The quarrymen cut the statue first and the prayers second. When both are finished, the statue stands up by itself.
lore.egyptian_desert_colossus.upgradeLore: The Divine Colossi carry gold in their joints. It is said to be what lets them lift a whole doorway and throw it.

lore.japanese_kitsune.sourceNote: Kitsune are fox spirits of Japanese folklore, associated with Inari shrines; tales credit old foxes with more tails, wisdom and magic.
sourceRefs: Inari shrine traditions; Konjaku Monogatari fox tales — to be verified
lore.japanese_kitsune.gameLore: The foxes of the grove bring rice to the shrine steps in good years. In bad years they bring the soldiers instead.
lore.japanese_kitsune.upgradeLore: A fox that has grown nine tails remembers every favour it has ever owed, and pays them at the worst moment for its enemies.

lore.japanese_kappa.sourceNote: The kappa is a water creature of Japanese folklore, often described with a shell and a water-filled hollow on its head; tales say it keeps its word once a promise is made.
sourceRefs: Edo-period yōkai compendia (e.g. Toriyama Sekien) — to be verified
lore.japanese_kappa.gameLore: The kappa agreed to guard the town’s river crossings in return for cucumbers and courtesy. Travellers still bow to the water before they wade in.
lore.japanese_kappa.upgradeLore: The River Elders made that agreement themselves. They are very strict about the bowing.

lore.japanese_tengu.sourceNote: Tengu are mountain spirits of Japanese folklore, pictured as bird-like or long-nosed winged beings; legends tell of tengu teaching swordsmanship to heroes.
sourceRefs: Legends of Mount Kurama and Minamoto no Yoshitsune — to be verified
lore.japanese_tengu.gameLore: The tengu train anyone who can climb to their nest. Few can. The ones who manage it come down very quickly.
lore.japanese_tengu.upgradeLore: Great Tengu taught the teachers. They still correct the stance of anyone who fights near them.

lore.japanese_oni.sourceNote: Oni are ogre-like beings of Japanese folklore, often shown horned and carrying an iron club (kanabō); the Momotarō tale ends on an island of oni.
sourceRefs: Momotarō folktale; yōkai picture scrolls — to be verified
lore.japanese_oni.gameLore: The oni of the quarry were defeated long ago, and they have never forgotten that the victor fed them afterwards. They work for rice and a good fight.
lore.japanese_oni.upgradeLore: An Oni Warlord wears the armor of the general who beat him. He considers it a compliment to them both.

lore.japanese_jorogumo.sourceNote: The jorōgumo is a spider yōkai of Japanese folklore said to take the form of a woman; the name is also that of a real orb-weaving spider.
sourceRefs: Edo-period tales (e.g. Taihei-Hyakumonogatari) — to be verified
lore.japanese_jorogumo.gameLore: The hollow behind the castle is thick with silk. The castle pays its rent there in lantern oil and does not send anyone to collect.
lore.japanese_jorogumo.upgradeLore: The Queen has spun for four hundred years. Her silk can hold a falling wall.

lore.japanese_kirin.sourceNote: The kirin (Chinese qilin) is an auspicious hooved chimera said to appear in the reign of a just ruler; Japanese art often gives it scales and flames.
sourceRefs: East Asian qilin tradition; Japanese shrine carvings — to be verified
lore.japanese_kirin.gameLore: A kirin never steps on a living blade of grass. The castle built it a pavilion of stone so it would have somewhere to stand.
lore.japanese_kirin.upgradeLore: The Celestial Kirin came down from the clouds when a fair lord took the castle. It has not decided yet whether to stay.

lore.japanese_orochi.sourceNote: Yamata no Orochi is the eight-headed, eight-tailed serpent slain by the storm god Susanoo in the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki; the sword Kusanagi was found in one of its tails.
sourceRefs: Kojiki; Nihon Shoki — to be verified
lore.japanese_orochi.gameLore: The sanctuary keeps eight vats of rice wine filled. Nobody asks what happens if one of them runs dry.
lore.japanese_orochi.upgradeLore: The Imperial Orochi are older than the story. They consider it slander.

lore.celtic_pooka.sourceNote: The púca is a shape-changing spirit of Irish folklore, often appearing as a dark horse, goat or hare; it can bring either fortune or trouble.
sourceRefs: Irish folklore collections (e.g. Crofton Croker, Yeats) — to be verified
lore.celtic_pooka.gameLore: Nobody invites the pooka to the muster. They arrive anyway, in whatever shape suits the weather, and nobody has ever dared send them home.
lore.celtic_pooka.upgradeLore: An Elder Pooka has been a horse, a goat, an eagle and once, briefly, a cart. It knows which shape a spear hates most.

lore.celtic_cu_sith.sourceNote: The cù-sìth is a large otherworldly hound of Scottish Highland folklore, often described as dark green; its baying was taken as an omen.
sourceRefs: Scottish Highland folklore collections — to be verified
lore.celtic_cu_sith.gameLore: The hounds hunt the hill paths at night. Travellers who hear them bay three times are advised to be inside by the third.
lore.celtic_cu_sith.upgradeLore: The Great Hounds answer only to whoever holds the hall. They have outlived eleven chieftains so far.

lore.celtic_kelpie.sourceNote: The kelpie is a shape-shifting water horse of Scottish folklore said to haunt rivers and lochs and lure riders into the water.
sourceRefs: Scottish folklore; the Kelpies sculpture (Falkirk) as a modern reference — to be verified
lore.celtic_kelpie.gameLore: Nobody rides a kelpie. The fort’s warriors run alongside them into battle, and let go of the mane before the water.
lore.celtic_kelpie.upgradeLore: Dread Kelpies come from the loch that has no bottom. They do not stop for anything, including walls.

lore.celtic_banshee.sourceNote: The bean sídhe ("woman of the fairy mound") of Irish folklore is a spirit whose keening foretells a death in certain families.
sourceRefs: Irish folklore collections — to be verified
lore.celtic_banshee.gameLore: The cairn women keen for the fort’s dead. In war they keen for the enemy’s, a little early.
lore.celtic_banshee.upgradeLore: A Battle Banshee has cried for so many warriors that she knows exactly where the next one will fall.

lore.celtic_selkie.sourceNote: Selkies are seal-folk of Scottish, Irish and Faroese folklore who shed their sealskins to walk on land.
sourceRefs: Orkney and Shetland tales; Faroese Kópakonan legend — to be verified
lore.celtic_selkie.gameLore: The cove folk keep their skins hidden under the stones. The fort keeps the stones guarded, and the selkies keep the coast.
lore.celtic_selkie.upgradeLore: Storm Selkies come in only when the winter sea is at its worst. They bring a little of it with them.

lore.celtic_horned_stag_spirit.sourceNote: An antlered figure appears in Celtic art, most famously on the Gundestrup cauldron; he is often identified with Cernunnos, and white stags lead heroes into the otherworld in many tales.
sourceRefs: Gundestrup cauldron; Pillar of the Boatmen inscription — to be verified
lore.celtic_horned_stag_spirit.gameLore: The stags of the grove choose which hunters may enter the wood. The chosen ones come back with antler-shaped scars and very few words.
lore.celtic_horned_stag_spirit.upgradeLore: The Great Stag has never been hunted. It has, however, hunted.

lore.celtic_fomorian_giant.sourceNote: The Fomorians (Fomóire) are a hostile supernatural race of Irish myth, enemies of the Tuatha Dé Danann in the Lebor Gabála Érenn and the Cath Maige Tuired; Balor of the Evil Eye was their leader.
sourceRefs: Lebor Gabála Érenn; Cath Maige Tuired — to be verified
lore.celtic_fomorian_giant.gameLore: The Fomorians lost their war with the gods and went back to the sea. Some of them came back out when the fort offered them a hill of their own.
lore.celtic_fomorian_giant.upgradeLore: The Ancient Fomorians remember the war. They fight as if it never ended.

lore.mesoamerican_feathered_serpent.sourceNote: The feathered serpent is a deity and motif found across Mesoamerica — Quetzalcoatl among the Nahua, Kukulkan among the Maya — shown on temples such as Teotihuacan’s Temple of the Feathered Serpent.
sourceRefs: Temple of the Feathered Serpent, Teotihuacan; Chichen Itza — to be verified
lore.mesoamerican_feathered_serpent.gameLore: The serpents nest in the temple eaves. The priests count them at each new moon and plan the year by the number.
lore.mesoamerican_feathered_serpent.upgradeLore: Celestial serpents are the ones that learned to fly. The priests say they are practising to become something larger.

lore.mesoamerican_jaguar_spirit.sourceNote: The jaguar was a symbol of power, night and rulership across Mesoamerica; Aztec jaguar warriors (ocelomeh) were an elite military order.
sourceRefs: Florentine Codex; Maya royal iconography — to be verified
lore.mesoamerican_jaguar_spirit.gameLore: The jaguars of the prowl choose their own warriors. The warriors wear the spotted skin afterwards, and the jaguars seem to find that funny.
lore.mesoamerican_jaguar_spirit.upgradeLore: Sun Jaguars hunt when the others sleep. They do not need the dark to be unseen.

lore.mesoamerican_eagle_warrior_spirit.sourceNote: Eagle warriors (cuauhtli) were, with the jaguar warriors, one of the elite military orders of the Aztec state, associated with the sun.
sourceRefs: House of the Eagles, Templo Mayor; Florentine Codex — to be verified
lore.mesoamerican_eagle_warrior_spirit.gameLore: An eagle warrior who dies facing the sun is said to fly with it for four years. The spirits in the aerie are the ones who came back early to help.
lore.mesoamerican_eagle_warrior_spirit.upgradeLore: Solar Eagle Warriors finished their four years and chose to return anyway.

lore.mesoamerican_cenote_crocodile.sourceNote: Cenotes are natural sinkholes of the Yucatán, some of them sacred (e.g. the Sacred Cenote at Chichen Itza); in Maya myth the earth itself was sometimes pictured as a great crocodile.
sourceRefs: Sacred Cenote, Chichen Itza; Maya cosmology studies — to be verified
lore.mesoamerican_cenote_crocodile.gameLore: The cenote under the city goes down to the underworld, and something down there keeps the water clean. The priests feed it so it will keep doing so.
lore.mesoamerican_cenote_crocodile.upgradeLore: A Temple Crocodile has lived in the temple pool since before the temple. It thinks of the priests as its keepers, not the other way round.

lore.mesoamerican_camazotz.sourceNote: Camazotz ("death bat") appears in the K’iche’ Maya Popol Vuh, where the Hero Twins must survive the House of Bats in Xibalba.
sourceRefs: Popol Vuh — to be verified
lore.mesoamerican_camazotz.gameLore: The bat cave is the one place in the city where no lamp is ever lit. The Camazotz like it that way, and they guard the city at night in return.
lore.mesoamerican_camazotz.upgradeLore: On a blood moon the Camazotz fly higher and come back later. The city stays indoors.

lore.mesoamerican_xiuhcoatl.sourceNote: Xiuhcoatl, the "turquoise" or "fire serpent", was the weapon of Huitzilopochtli in Aztec myth and a common motif on the Sun Stone.
sourceRefs: Aztec Calendar Stone; Florentine Codex — to be verified
lore.mesoamerican_xiuhcoatl.gameLore: The fire serpents sleep coiled around the new-fire altar. When the city lights its fires every fifty-two years, the serpents are the first to wake.
lore.mesoamerican_xiuhcoatl.upgradeLore: A Divine Xiuhcoatl has been thrown by a god. It remembers the arc, and it still enjoys it.

lore.mesoamerican_stone_colossus.sourceNote: Monumental stone warrior columns such as the Atlantes of Tula (Toltec) stood atop temple platforms; Olmec colossal heads are older examples of monumental sculpture.
sourceRefs: Atlantes of Tula; Olmec colossal heads — to be verified
lore.mesoamerican_stone_colossus.gameLore: The colossi stood on the pyramid roof holding it up. When the city needed them, the priests built new columns first.
lore.mesoamerican_stone_colossus.upgradeLore: A Sun Colossus has the day’s light sealed inside it. It is warm to the touch, even at midnight.

lore.brigand.sourceNote: Bandits on trade roads are a common figure in many cultures; no single tradition is adapted.
lore.brigand.gameLore: Where kingdoms quarrel, roads go unwatched. Brigands are deserters, debtors and the hungry, holding a ford or a pass until someone pays. They answer to whoever paid last.
lore.brigand.upgradeLore: Cutthroats are the brigands who lived long enough to choose their ambushes.

lore.hill_slinger.sourceNote: Ancient writers describe slingers from the Balearic Islands and other hill peoples serving as hired troops. Folklore inspiration only; the game creature, its numbers and its story are an original adaptation.
sourceRefs: Diodorus Siculus, Library of History, book 5 (the Balearic slingers)
lore.hill_slinger.gameLore: In the hill country every child learns the sling before the plough: wolves do not wait for a soldier. The flocks are thin in winter, and a war band pays in silver.
lore.hill_slinger.upgradeLore: Sling Masters cast shaped lead bullets that fly farther than stones and land harder.

lore.wild_boar.sourceNote: Wild boars are dangerous game in many hunting traditions. Folklore inspiration only; the game creature, its numbers and its story are an original adaptation.
lore.wild_boar.gameLore: The oak woods belong to the boars. A herd defends its ground with a running charge, and a sounder can scatter a column of spearmen.
lore.wild_boar.upgradeLore: The great tuskers are old boars that have outlived every hunt sent for them.

lore.clay_golem.sourceNote: Jewish folklore tells of the golem, a figure of clay brought to life to serve and protect, best known from later legends set in Prague. Folklore inspiration only; the game creature, its numbers and its story are an original adaptation.
sourceRefs: General folklore reference — golem legends
lore.clay_golem.gameLore: Some forgotten workshop pressed a sigil into wet clay and fired it in a kiln. The figures still keep the last order they were given — guard the door — long after the door has fallen.
lore.clay_golem.upgradeLore: Bronze Golems were sheathed by a later smith who wanted his treasury safe from charges.

lore.wyvern.sourceNote: The wyvern — a two-legged winged dragon — is a figure of European heraldry. Folklore inspiration only; the game creature, its numbers and its story are an original adaptation.
sourceRefs: General reference — the wyvern in European heraldry
lore.wyvern.gameLore: Wyverns nest on sea cliffs and quarry walls. They hunt goats, sheep and the occasional shepherd, and they do not share a sky with griffins.
lore.wyvern.upgradeLore: Matriarchs guard the egg ledges and answer every attack on the nest.

lore.ogre.sourceNote: Ogres are man-eating giants of European fairy tales. Folklore inspiration only; the game creature, its numbers and its story are an original adaptation.
sourceRefs: General reference — the ogre in European fairy tales
lore.ogre.gameLore: Ogres keep to the high valleys and come down when the herds fail. They fight for whoever feeds them and walk away when the meat runs out.
lore.ogre.upgradeLore: A chieftain rules by beating every challenger; it has learned to hit back before the second blow lands.

lore.basilisk.sourceNote: Pliny the Elder describes the basilisk as a small, deadly crowned serpent; medieval bestiaries made it a king of serpents. Folklore inspiration only; the game creature, its numbers and its story are an original adaptation.
sourceRefs: Pliny the Elder, Natural History, book 8 (the basilisk)
lore.basilisk.gameLore: The stories say a basilisk kills with a look. The truth is plainer: its hide turns blades and its bite is enough. Desert caravans pay guides to steer wide of their dens.
lore.basilisk.upgradeLore: The greater basilisks are old enough that spears break on them and charges stall.

lore.elder_drake.sourceNote: The hoard-guarding dragon is old in northern European poetry (the dragon of Beowulf). Folklore inspiration only; the game creature, its numbers and its story are an original adaptation.
sourceRefs: Beowulf (the dragon episode)
lore.elder_drake.gameLore: Elder Drakes sleep on gold that was minted by kingdoms nobody remembers. A drake that wakes takes a season to sleep again, and the country around it burns in the meantime.
lore.elder_drake.upgradeLore: The ancient ones answer every blow; no hero has struck one twice unanswered.

celtic_fiachra.name: Fiachra
celtic_fiachra.title: The Usurper of the Ford
celtic_fiachra.biography: A chieftain who took the high seat in the long winter and keeps it with the Withered King’s help. Rival empire in The Silver Branch, mission 5.

celtic_corc.name: Corc
celtic_corc.title: Raider of the Grey Sea
celtic_corc.biography: A sea-raider who came with the mist and stayed for the plunder. Patrol in The Silver Branch, mission 4.

provenance.note: Campaign character (owner request 2026-10-02: campaigns for the four remaining pantheons).

specialty.name: Selkies
specialty.summary: Selkies and Storm Selkies in this hero’s army: +1 Attack and +1 Defense in battle, one more of each at hero levels 4 and 8.

celtic_tadhg.name: Tadhg the Grey
celtic_tadhg.title: Champion of the Withered King
celtic_tadhg.biography: The Withered King’s champion, who holds the stags’ wood. The Silver Branch, mission 6.

provenance.note: Campaign character (owner request 2026-10-02: campaigns for the four remaining pantheons).

specialty.name: Pooka
specialty.summary: Pooka and Elder Pooka in this hero’s army: +1 Attack and +1 Defense in battle, one more of each at hero levels 4 and 8.

celtic_ciar.name: Ciar
celtic_ciar.title: Warden of the Mound
celtic_ciar.biography: Keeper of the road between the summer stone and the winter stone. Patrol in The Silver Branch, mission 7.

provenance.note: Campaign character (owner request 2026-10-02: campaigns for the four remaining pantheons).

specialty.name: Banshees
specialty.summary: Banshees and Battle Banshees in this hero’s army: +1 Attack and +1 Defense in battle, one more of each at hero levels 4 and 8.

mesoamerican_itzel.name: Itzel
mesoamerican_itzel.title: Day-Keeper of Xochitla
mesoamerican_itzel.biography: A day-keeper who counts the calendar and knows which fire belongs to which day. The hero of The New Fire.

provenance.note: Campaign character (owner request 2026-10-02: campaigns for the four remaining pantheons).
